## Methods

Animal ethics and housing conditions
All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Hainan University (Approval No. HNUAUCC-2023-00190) and were conducted in strict accordance with the Guidelines for the Care and Use of Experimental Animals of Hainan University. Germ-free mice were maintained in sterile isolators, while specific pathogen-free (SPF) mice were housed in SPF animal facilities. All mice were kept under a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle and housed individually, with a controlled ambient temperature of 25 ± 2 °C and relative humidity of 55 ± 5%.

Calcium precipitation assay for bile salt hydrolase activity
Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis (B. animalis subsp. lactis) strains were obtained from the Tropical Probiotics Development and Utilization Team at Hainan University, which were originally isolated from the intestinal tracts of healthy infants.

To screen for B. animalis subsp. lactis strains with bile acid-metabolizing capacity, 12 randomly selected strains were subjected to a calcium precipitation assay to evaluate their bile salt hydrolase activity. Briefly, 50 µL of each overnight culture was spotted onto MRS-cysteine (MRS-cys) agar supplemented with 0.1% cysteine·HCl, 3.0 g/L taurodeoxycholic acid sodium salt, 3.0 g/L glycodeoxycholic acid sodium salt, 2.0 g/L sodium thioglycolate, and 0.37 g/L anhydrous CaCl₂. Plates were incubated anaerobically at 37 °C for 48 h, after which the diameter of the calcium precipitation halo (indicative of bile salt hydrolase activity) was measured. MRS-cys agar without bile acids served as the negative control. All assays were performed in triplicate.

Bile salt hydrolases specific activity assay
To determine the BSH-specific activity of the candidate strains, we applied the classical ninhydrin colorimetric assay to quantify released amino acids55, a well-established method for amino acid measurement that indirectly reflects BSH hydrolysis efficiency. Specifically, overnight cultures of candidate strains were harvested at mid-log phase and thoroughly mixed. A 1 mL aliquot of culture was centrifuged at 3000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C, and the supernatant was discarded. The cell pellet was washed twice with 200 µL of ice-cold 0.1 M PBS (pH 6.0) and then resuspended in 500 µL of PBS (pH 6.0) to prepare a concentrated cell suspension.

BSH-specific activity was then assayed using glycine-conjugated bile acids (10 mM) as the substrate. In each reaction, 100 µL of the prepared cell suspension was mixed with 100 µL of substrate solution, and the final volume was adjusted to 1 mL with PBS (pH 6.0). Mixtures were incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. In parallel, blank controls contained 100 µL of cell suspension and 900 µL of PBS (no substrate). At the end of the incubation, 500 µL of 15% trichloroacetic acid was added to terminate the reaction, followed by 3 min of incubation at room temperature. Samples were then centrifuged at 14,000 × g for 10 min, and the supernatant was transferred to a 15 mL tube. To each supernatant, 1.5 mL of ninhydrin reagent was added and gently mixed before heating in a boiling water bath for 15 min. Tubes were immediately cooled on ice for 3 min, and absorbance was measured at 570 nm. Released amino acid concentrations were calculated against a concurrently prepared standard curve.

Simultaneously, total protein concentration in the crude lysate was determined using the Bradford assay with bovine serum albumin (BSA) as the standard. Specific activity (U/mg) was defined as the micromoles of amino acid released per milligram of protein per minute, and calculated using the following formula:

Specific activity (U·mg⁻¹) = Amount of amino acid produced (μmol) / (Protein content (mg) × Reaction time (min)) (1)

To assess functional enhancement in evolved strains relative to their parental counterparts, we calculated the fold change in BSH activity as follows:

Fold change = Cₙ / C₀ (2)

where Cₙ is the Specific activity by the nth induced strain, and C₀ is the corresponding value for its original strain (n = 1, 2, ..., 60).

Assessment of tolerance and growth performance
To comprehensively evaluate the gut-survival potential of these 12 candidate strains, we assessed their acid tolerance, bile acid tolerance, and growth performance. For acid and bile acid tolerance assays, strains were grown to mid-log phase and then transferred (2% v/v) into modified MRS-cys broth: one set adjusted to pH 2.0 (acid tolerance) and another supplemented with 0.3% (w/v) bovine bile (bile acid tolerance). Acid-treated cultures were incubated anaerobically at 37 °C for 2 h, and bile acid-treated cultures for 4 h, with untreated cultures in MRS-cys as controls. After incubation, OD₆₀₀ was measured in both treated and control groups, and survival rates (%) were calculated. As for growth performance, activated cultures were inoculated at 2% (v/v) into MRS-cys broth and incubated anaerobically at 37 °C for 36 h. OD₆₀₀ measurements were taken every 4 h, with uninoculated medium serving as the control.

In vitro induction experiment
To specifically enhance bile acid-metabolizing capacity, each candidate strain was first inoculated into 25 mL of MRS-cys broth and incubated anaerobically at 37 °C until reaching the logarithmic growth phase. At that point, 2% (v/v) of the culture was transferred into an equal volume of fresh MRS-cys medium supplemented with 0.3% (w/v) conjugated bile acids (a 1:1 mixture of sodium glycodeoxycholate and sodium taurodeoxycholate) and incubated anaerobically for 24 h. This serial passaging (using a 2% (v/v) inoculum each time) was repeated for ten consecutive rounds. After the tenth passage, the evolved population was diluted and plated onto solid MRS-cys agar. Subsequently, 60 colonies were randomly selected and assayed for BSH-specific activity to evaluate the effectiveness of the in vitro induction.

Host-mediated in vivo induction
To implement the in vivo adaptation strategy, we employed GF mice as an evolution bioreactor to eliminate interference from endogenous microbial strains. Male GF C57BL/6J mice (7 weeks old; n = 4) were obtained from Shenzhen Jingtai Biotech (Guangdong, China) and maintained in sterile isolators on irradiated standard chow for 7 days. To establish colonization by B. animalis subsp. lactis H22B656, each mouse received a 200 µL oral gavage of a 10⁹ CFU suspension once daily for three consecutive days. Following colonization, mice were subjected to a stepwise high-fat high-cholesterol dietary regimen over a 7-week induction period: weeks 1–3 on chow containing 30% fat and 0.2% cholesterol; weeks 3–5 on 45% fat and 0.2% cholesterol; and weeks 5–7 on 60% fat and 0.2% cholesterol.

To isolate adapted strains from GF mice, fresh stool samples were aseptically collected at the end of weeks 1, 3, 5, and 7, immediately suspended in 1.5 mL of sterile saline, and thoroughly homogenized under anaerobic conditions. Homogenates were serially diluted to 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁶ and plated on MRS-cys agar. After anaerobic incubation at 37 °C for 24 h, colonies from an appropriate dilution were randomly picked.

To ensure a representative evaluation of the adaptation process, 15 isolates were randomly selected from the plates of each sampling time point (Weeks 1, 3, 5, and 7), resulting in a total library of 60 induced isolates. These isolates were inoculated into MRS-cys liquid medium, labeled sequentially, and stored at –80 °C for subsequent analyses. Finally, 60 induced isolates were assayed alongside the original B. animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 for BSH-specific activity to evaluate the efficacy of the host-mediated in vivo induction.

Intervention diets
The normal diet (ND) was designed in accordance with established nutritional guidelines and comprised casein, corn starch, lard, vitamins, minerals, and fiber, providing a balanced mix of protein, fat, and carbohydrates. To generate an intestinal high-bile-acid environment in GF mice, we formulated a high-fat/high-cholesterol diet by increasing lard content to supply 30%, 45%, or 60% of energy from fat and supplementing with 0.2% cholesterol. For the NAFLD intervention study, a high-fat diet (HFAD) was similarly prepared from the normal diet to provide 60% energy from fat, without cholesterol supplementation. All diets were sterilized by γ irradiation and provided by Anhui Kuibu Shuyu Biotechnology Co., Ltd. Full dietary compositions are listed in Supplementary Data 2.

Genome assembly and annotation of the original strain
To obtain the complete reference genome of the original strain B. animalis subsp. lactis H22B656, genomic DNA was extracted from pure cultures of B. animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 using the QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen), following the manufacturer’s protocol. DNA concentration and integrity were assessed by NanoDrop spectrophotometry (A260/A280 ≈ 1.8) and 0.8% agarose gel electrophoresis. Samples meeting these quality criteria were sent to Beijing Novogene Bioinformatics Technology Co., Ltd. for third-generation long-read sequencing on the Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) PromethION platform.

Nanopore libraries were prepared using the ONT Ligation Sequencing Kit (Oxford Nanopore Technologies) as follows: Genomic DNA integrity was assessed by gel electrophoresis and quantified using a Qubit fluorometer. The DNA underwent end-repair and A-tailing reactions, after which sequencing adapters and motor proteins were ligated to both ends. Unligated molecules were removed via purification steps, and libraries meeting quality standards were sequenced on the PromethION platform. Sample B. animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 generated 433,564 raw reads with a total output of 2.4 Gb.

For genome assembly, raw reads were first demultiplexed and adapter-trimmed to generate subreads, which were then filtered to retain only those ≥ 50 bp in length. De novo assembly of the filtered subreads was performed with Canu56 (v2.2). The resulting draft contigs were polished through three rounds of alignment and consensus correction by coupling Minimap257 (v2.22) and Racon58 (v1.4.13, command: minimap2 -t 40 assembly.fasta pass.fastq.gz > round1.paf; racon -t 4 pass.fastq.gz round1.paf assembly.fasta > round1.fasta).

Gene prediction and functional annotation of the complete genome were performed with Prokka59 v1.14.6 (command: prokka --outdir test --prefix test test.fa). Predicted proteins were further annotated via the KEGG Automatic Annotation Server60 (KAAS v4.0; http://www.genome.jp/tools/kaas/), using the bi-directional best hit method for pathway assignment. To further annotate hypothetical proteins, BLASTp searches were also conducted with NCBI BLAST+ v2.16.0 against the non-redundant (nr) protein database (e-value ≤ 1e-5, identity ≥ 30%, query coverage ≥ 70%, up to 20 alignments; command: blastp -query query.faa -db nr -out blast.tsv -outfmt 6 -evalue 1e-5 -num_threads 24 -num_alignments 20).

Whole genome sequencing of the adapted strains
To investigate the genetic basis of its enhanced bile acid-metabolizing capacity, we performed whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of the adapted strain W5S9. Genomic DNA from purified W5S9 cultures was extracted and assessed for its purity (A260/A280 = 1.8-2.0) and fragment integrity (>20 kb). DNA was then randomly sheared to the desired fragment size using a Covaris ultrasonicator. Fragmented DNA underwent end repair and 3’ A-tailing, followed by ligation of Illumina sequencing adapters. Adapter-ligated libraries were size-selected to remove off-target fragments, PCR-amplified to enrich adapter-containing molecules, and purified to eliminate residual contaminants. Equimolar libraries were pooled and sequenced by Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China) using an Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform (2 × 150 bp paired-end). Raw reads were stringently filtered for quality using fastp61 v0.23.2. Sample W5S9 yielded 8,310,066 raw reads, of which 8,289,624 high-quality reads were retained after filtering.

SNVs calling
To accurately capture genetic variants acquired during in vivo adaptation, we performed SNV calling on WGS data using two complementary pipelines (inStrain30 v1.0.0 and BCFtools31 v 1.21) and retained only the intersection of their call sets for downstream analysis. First, WGS data were aligned to the original H22B656 reference genome with Bowtie262 v2.5.4. Alignments were converted to coordinate-sorted, indexed BAM files using SAMtools31 v1.22. SNV detection was then carried out independently with: (1) inStrain (command: inStrain profile sample.bam ref.fna -c 100 -f 0.49 -o sample.profile -p 24 -g ref_genes.fna); (2) BCFtools (command: bcftools mpileup -C 50 -Ou -m 3 -F 0.0002 -f ref.fa sorted.bam | bcftools call -mv -Ob -o variants.bcf). High-confidence SNVs were defined as variants identified by both methods. We identified a total of 282 high-confidence SNVs in the adapted strain W5S9. The distribution of SNVs across the genome was plotted using the R package circlize (version 0.4.15, Fig. 3a).

Promoter prediction for non-coding SNVs
To determine whether SNVs in non-coding regions might influence downstream gene expression, we conducted promoter prediction and target-gene association analyses for all intergenic SNVs. First, each SNV’s nearest gene was identified using BEDTools63 v2.18, and the distance to the gene’s transcription start site (TSS) was calculated. Genes located on the same strand, with SNVs positioned within 0–300 bp upstream of their TSS, were selected as candidate regulatory targets. Promoter regions encompassing each candidate SNV were then predicted using BPROM (www.softberry.com), and the predicted promoter elements were inspected for canonical −10/−35 motifs to evaluate their regulatory potential.

Transcriptome sequencing and data analysis
To identify key genes with expression changes caused by genetic variants acquired during in vivo adaptation, we performed transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq) on the original strain H22B656 and the adapted strain W5S9. Briefly, each strain was cultured anaerobically for 12 h in MRS-cys broth supplemented with 0.3% conjugated bile acid (sodium glycodeoxycholate and sodium taurodeoxycholate). Cultures were centrifuged at 1500 × g for 30 min, and pellets were immediately processed for RNA extraction.

Total RNA was isolated using a Qiagen RNeasy kit, and integrity (RIN > 8) and purity (A260/A280: 1.8-2.0) were confirmed by agarose gel electrophoresis and NanoDrop spectrophotometry. Ribosomal RNA was depleted, and the remaining RNA was purified by ethanol precipitation. First-strand cDNA synthesis was primed with random hexamers, and second-strand synthesis incorporated dUTP to preserve strand specificity. The resulting double-stranded cDNA underwent end repair, 3’ A-tailing, adapter ligation, size selection, USER enzyme digestion to remove the dUTP-containing strand, PCR enrichment, and bead-based purification to yield strand-specific libraries. Library concentration was measured by Qubit and qPCR, and fragment size distribution was assessed on an Agilent Bioanalyzer. Libraries meeting quality thresholds were pooled equimolarly and sequenced (2 × 150 bp) on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 by Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China).

Raw data were quality-filtered with fastp v0.23.2 to remove adapter contamination, trim low-quality bases (Q < 20), and discard reads containing ambiguous nucleotides (N), resulting in high-quality clean reads for downstream analysis. Sequencing of six transcriptomics samples yielded an average of 11.95 ± 0.15 million raw reads and 11.79 ± 0.15 million clean reads per sample (mean ± SEM). Transcript-level quantification was performed with Salmon64 v1.9.0 against the reference transcriptome (salmon quant -i mg -l A -1 test_1.fastq.gz -2 test_2.fastq.gz -o test.quant). Differential expression analysis between the original and adapted strains was performed in R (v4.4.1) using the DESeq2 (v1.44.0) package (n = 3 per strain, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction; FDR < 0.001 and |log₂FC| > 0.4), and the resulting differential features were visualized as volcano plots using OmicShare (https://www.omicshare.com/; Fig. 3c, d). Gene expression differences between adapted and original strains for cbh and mdr were shown as bar charts in GraphPad Prism v10 (Fig. 3f, g).

Validation of identified SNVs by targeted Sanger sequencing
To validate the candidate SNVs (rs1846941 and rs402499) identified by WGS, we designed locus-specific primer pairs (mrd-F/mrd-R and rs1846941-f/ rs1846941-r; Supplementary Data 3) to amplify 200 bp regions centered on each variant (100 bp upstream and downstream). Purified PCR products were submitted to Beijing Qinke Biotechnology Co., Ltd. for Sanger sequencing. Following sequencing, the raw reads were aligned against the B. animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 reference genome to verify the target mutations. Sequence visualization and variant confirmation were performed using Geneious Prime v2022.2 (Fig. 4a, b).

Determination of the genetic stability of key SNVs
To verify the genetic stability of key SNVs in the adapted strain, we conducted a rigorous long-term continuous passage experiment followed by whole genome sequencing (WGS). Specifically, the adapted strain W5S9 was subjected to daily serial passaging for 4 weeks under two conditions: (i) a non-selective medium (MRS broth supplemented with L-cysteine hydrochloride), used to assess stability in the absence of selection pressure; and (ii) a selective medium (MRS broth supplemented with bile salts and L-cysteine hydrochloride), used to mimic gut environmental pressure. Target strains were re-isolated weekly, genomic DNA was extracted, and WGS was performed to monitor potential genetic changes (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Reporter plasmid construction and fluorescence assays
To assess the regulatory impact of SNVs rs1846941 and rs402499 on target gene expression, we constructed mCherry and EGFP reporter plasmids harboring either the wild-type or variant sequences.

For SNV rs1846941 located in the non-coding region, we PCR-amplified 100 bp fragments (50 bp upstream and downstream) carrying either the wild-type or rs1846941 allele from genomic DNA of the original H22B656 and the adapted W5S9 strains, respectively. Each non-coding fragment was fused to mCherry by overlap-extension PCR, and the resulting expression cassettes were cloned into the EcoRI site of pLH01. Recombinant plasmids were introduced into B. animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 by electroporation. Single colonies were then grown anaerobically at 37 °C in MRS-cys medium (supplemented with 2% glucose, 10 µg/mL chloramphenicol, and 0.3% (w/v) conjugated sodium deoxycholate, sodium cholate, or sodium chenodeoxycholate) to an OD₆₀₀ of ~0.5. Cells were then harvested, washed twice with PBS, and fluorescence was measured on a BioTek Synergy H1 multimode plate reader.

For SNV rs402499 located in the coding region (in mdr), wild-type and N192D gene-egfp fusions were assembled by overlap-extension PCR and cloned into SalI/XhoI–linearized pET28a. Plasmids were transformed into E. coli BL21 (DE3) by heat shock. Transformants were cultured in LB medium (with 0.3% conjugated sodium deoxycholate, conjugated sodium cholate, or conjugated sodium chenodeoxycholate and 50 µg/mL kanamycin) at 37 °C to OD₆₀₀ = 0.6–0.8. After harvesting and two PBS washes, fluorescence was recorded on the Synergy H1. Statistical analyses and data visualization were performed using GraphPad Prism v10. For Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 2, multiple two-tailed Mann–Whitney tests were used to compare H22B656 and W5S9 (n = 3 independent samples per group), and multiple comparisons were controlled using a two-stage step-up false discovery rate (FDR) procedure with Q = 1%.

Construction of gene knockout and complemented strains
To establish a causal relationship between the rs1846941 and rs402499 mutations and the phenotype of interest, we employed a homologous recombination strategy using the temperature-sensitive suicide plasmid pKO403 to generate deletion mutants targeting the mdr and cbh promoter regions in both the parental strain Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 and the adapted strain B. animalis subsp. lactis W5S9. Genomic DNA from the respective strains was used as the template to amplify the upstream and downstream homologous arms flanking the mdr gene and cbh promoter regions by PCR using primers listed in Supplementary Data 3. Amplicons were resolved by agarose gel electrophoresis and purified. The pKO403 plasmid was linearized by double digestion with SalI and BamHI and seamlessly assembled with the purified homologous arms using 2× Ezmax® Universal CloneMix (37 °C, 30 min). Assembly products were transformed into E. coli DH5α competent cells, and recombinant plasmids were identified by colony PCR. Plasmids confirmed by PCR were isolated and electroporated into electrocompetent H22B656 and W5S9 cells (2.1 kV, 200 Ω, 25 µF). Following electroporation, cells were recovered in 1 mL MRS-cys medium under anaerobic conditions at 37 °C for 4 h and plated on MRS-cys agar containing chloramphenicol (10 µg/mL) to select for single-crossover integrants. Chloramphenicol-resistant colonies were cultured in MRS-cys broth supplemented with chloramphenicol (10 µg/mL) at 37 °C for 48 h and subsequently plated on MRS-cys agar with chloramphenicol for anaerobic incubation at 42 °C for 48 h to promote double-crossover recombination. Successful deletion of the target region was confirmed by PCR, and double-crossover deletion mutants were obtained. To eliminate the pKO403 plasmid, verified mutants were passaged for three consecutive generations in antibiotic-free MRS-cys medium.

For complementation of the Δmdr mutant, a 1648-bp fragment containing the full-length mdr gene and its native promoter was PCR-amplified from the genomic DNA of H22B656 or W5S9 using primers listed in Supplementary Data 3 and cloned into SalI/BamHI-digested pKO403. The resulting plasmid was introduced into the Δmdr strain by electroporation, and transformants were selected on MRS-cys agar containing chloramphenicol (10 µg/mL). Successful construction of complemented strains was confirmed by PCR.

RT-qPCR gene expression analysis
To assess the impact of the rs402499 and rs1846941 variants on gene expression, bacterial cultures were grown in MRS-cys medium supplemented with 0.3% (w/v) conjugated sodium deoxycholate, sodium cholate, or sodium chenodeoxycholate. After 12 h of incubation, bacterial cells were collected for subsequent analysis. Total RNA was extracted with TRIzol reagent and treated with DNase I to remove genomic DNA. cDNA synthesis was performed using the PrimeScript™ RT kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The cycle threshold (Cₜ) values were normalized to the reference gene rplx to obtain ΔCₜ values. Relative gene expression was calculated using the comparative Cₜ method (2⁻ΔΔCT), with the wild-type Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 strain serving as the calibrator (relative expression = 1) for each bile salt condition independently. Statistical analyses were performed using R v4.4.1 software with the rstatix (v0.7.2) and ggpubr (v0.6.0) packages. Data are presented as mean ± SD, with individual data points from biological replicates overlaid (n = 3). Comparisons between strains under each bile salt condition were analyzed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s Honest Significant Difference (HSD) post-hoc test for multiple comparisons. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05 (Fig. 4d, f).

Bile acid stress survival assay for mdr phenotypic validation
To validate the contribution of mdr expression to bile acid tolerance, survival under bile acid stress was assessed by viable colony counting. The parental wild-type strain H22B656, the adapted wild-type strain W5S9, their isogenic mdr knockout mutants, and the corresponding complemented strains were grown overnight under standard culture conditions as described above. Cultures were harvested and adjusted to the same optical density, and equal aliquots were inoculated into fresh medium supplemented with 0.3% (w/v) cholic acid (CA), deoxycholic acid (DCA), or chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA). After incubation under bile acid stress, cultures were serially diluted and plated on bile acid–free agar. Colony-forming units (CFU) were counted after incubation, and survival was expressed as CFU per mL. Each condition was tested in three independent biological replicates, and data were analyzed by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD post hoc test (Fig. 4g).

Molecular docking analysis
To investigate the impact of the nonsynonymous variant rs402499 on MDR structure and its binding affinity for free bile acids, we used the AlphaFold server (https://alphafoldserver.com) to predict the three-dimensional structures of both wild-type and mutant MDR from their amino acid sequences, exporting the resulting models as PDB files for downstream analyses. The three-dimensional structures of deoxycholic acid (CID: 222528, https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Deoxycholic-acid), cholic acid (CID: 221493, https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Cholic-acid), and chenodeoxycholic acid (CID: 10133, https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Chenodeoxycholic-acid) were retrieved from PubChem, converted from SDF to PDBQT format with Open Babel (v3.1.1), and assigned Gasteiger charges.

Both wild-type and mutant MDR models were prepared for docking with AutoDockTools (v1.5.7) by removing crystallographic water molecules, adding hydrogens, and assigning Kollman charges before exporting them as PDBQT files. Potential ligand-binding pockets were identified using DoGSiteScorer (https://proteins.plus/). A ligand-centered docking grid was then defined (box size: 126³ Å³; grid spacing: 0.368 Å) and centered at coordinates x = -0.855, y = 10.657, z = -4.238 (dimensions: 20.33 × 20.33 × 20.33 Å³). Targeted molecular docking was performed with AutoDock Vina65 (v1.5.7). Statistical analyses and data visualization were performed using GraphPad Prism v10 (Fig. 4h). The binding pose with the lowest predicted binding energy was visualized in PyMOL (v2.5.4), and key ligand-receptor interactions, including hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic contacts, and shape complementarity, were analyzed (Fig. 4i).

Diet-induced NAFLD mouse model and probiotic gavage
To assess the beneficial potential of the adapted B. animalis subsp. lactis W5S9 in modulating host metabolism, we employed a diet-induced NAFLD mouse model in male SPF C57BL/6J mice (7 weeks old), based on the established link between bile acid dysregulation and NAFLD progression66. Mice were randomized into four groups (n = 6 per group): (1) Control (n = 6, normal diet, daily gavage with 200 µL sterile saline); (2) HFAD (n = 6, high-fat diet, daily gavage with 200 µL sterile saline); (3) HFAD-H22B656 (n = 6, high-fat diet, daily gavage with 200 µL sterile saline containing 10⁹ CFU of original strain B. animalis subsp. lactis H22B656); and (4) HFAD-W5S9 (n = 6, high-fat diet, daily gavage with 200 µL sterile saline containing 10⁹ CFU of adapted strain B. animalis subsp. lactis W5S9). The experiment lasted for 8 weeks. Body weight was measured weekly. At the end of the study, serum and liver tissues were collected for biochemical measurements and histopathological analysis to assess the preventive effects of the adapted and original strains on NAFLD. Additionally, fecal samples were collected for metagenomic sequencing and targeted bile acid metabolomics analysis.

Physiological and histopathological assessments
For the physiological markers assay, the levels of high-density lipoprotein (HDL-C), low-density lipoprotein (LDL-C), total triglycerides (TG), total cholesterol (TC), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), malondialdehyde (MDA), IL-6 and TNF-α in serum were measured according to the instructions of the ELISA kit (Shanghai Xinyu Biotechnology Co., Ltd.).

For histopathological analysis, liver specimens were rinsed in ice-cold sterile saline, and portions were either fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde or snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen. Sample processing, including paraffin embedding, sectioning, staining, and image capture, was performed by Wuhan Sewell Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (China). Semi-quantitative analysis of lipid droplet content was performed on Oil Red O-stained sections using Fiji (v2.17.0). Data visualization and statistical analyses were conducted in GraphPad Prism v10 using a Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test (n = 6 mice per group, Fig. 5i).

Whole metagenome sequencing and data analysis
To compare the effects of the adapted versus original strains on the gut microbiota composition in the diet-induced NAFLD mouse model, fresh stool samples were collected at the end of week 8 and immediately stored at −80 °C for whole metagenome sequencing (WMS). Genomic DNA was extracted using the QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen) and evaluated for integrity by 0.8% agarose gel electrophoresis, purity via A260/A280 ratios on a NanoDrop spectrophotometer, and concentration with a Qubit 2.0 fluorometer. Paired-end libraries (2 × 150 bp) were prepared and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform at Beijing Novogene Bioinformatics Technology Co., Ltd. Raw reads were quality-filtered using fastp v0.23.2 to remove adapter sequences and exclude read pairs with more than 50% of bases at Q ≤ 5 or over 10% ambiguous nucleotides (N bases). On average, each sample yielded 45.28 ± 0.56 million raw reads and 44.08 ± 0.57 million clean reads (mean ± SEM). Taxonomic profiling of the WMS data was performed using MetaPhlAn (v4.0.6)67 to identify microbial species and estimate their relative abundances. To specifically distinguish the direct enzymatic contribution of the supplemented strains from potential regulatory effects on the resident microbiota, we performed functional profiling of the metagenomic data using HUMAnN (v3.9) with the uniref90_koregrouping option to quantify the abundance of bile salt hydrolase (EC 3.5.1.24)–encoding genes (Supplementary Fig. 6).

qPCR quantification of B. animalis in fecal samples
To quantitatively assess the abundance of the original strain H22B656 and the adapted strain W5S9 in fecal samples, we designed H22B656-specific primers using the NCBI Primer-BLAST tool (H22BF: ACGGCACGATTCATGTGTCT; H22BR: CCAGATTCCATCCTCCTCGC). Fecal samples (0.1 g) were then subjected to DNA extraction using the TIANGEN Bacterial Genomic DNA Extraction Kit, and quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) was performed with the above primers. qPCR data were analyzed and visualized using GraphPad Prism v10, and statistical significance was evaluated using the Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test (Fig. 5c).

Targeted metabolomic profiling and data analysis of fecal bile acids
A total of 24 fecal samples (n = 6 biological replicates per group) were analyzed. Fecal bile acid extraction was performed using HPLC-grade acetonitrile and methanol (Merck) as solvents. Analytical standards (CNW, IsoReag, and Sigma-Aldrich) were prepared as 1 mg/mL stock solutions in methanol and stored at −20 °C. Working solutions were diluted to appropriate concentrations for calibration curves prior to analysis. Approximately 20 mg of ball-milled fecal sample was homogenized in 495 µL of methanol, spiked with 5 µL of internal standard solution (10 µg/mL), and subjected to protein precipitation at −20 °C. Following centrifugation at 13,200 × g for 10 min (4 °C) and filtration through a protein precipitation plate, supernatants were analyzed. To monitor instrument stability, quality control (QC) samples were prepared by pooling equal aliquots of all supernatants and analyzed every 10 samples.

Chromatographic separation was performed on an ExionLC™ AD UHPLC system (AB Sciex) equipped with a Waters HSS T3 C18 column (100 × 2.1 mm, 1.8 µm) maintained at 40 °C. Mobile phases consisted of (A) 0.01% acetic acid with 5 mmol/L ammonium acetate in water and (B) 0.01% acetic acid in acetonitrile. A linear gradient elution was performed at a flow rate of 0.35 mL/min: 5% to 40% B in 0–1 min; 40% to 50% B in 1–7 min; 50% to 75% B in 7–12 min; 75% to 95% B in 12–14 min; maintained at 95% B for 2 min (14–16 min); and re-equilibrated at 5% B from 16 to 17.5 min.

Mass spectrometric detection was conducted on an AB Sciex 6500+ QTRAP system coupled to an ExionLC™ AD UHPLC via electrospray ionization (ESI) in negative mode. Key parameters included: ion source temperature 550 °C, spray voltage −4500 V, and curtain gas 35 psi. Data acquisition employed scheduled multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) with Analyst software (v1.6.3), and quantification was performed using MultiQuant software (v3.0.3). Metabolites were identified by matching retention times and MS/MS spectra with the MetWare Database (MWDB) and authentic standards. Quantification was performed using MultiQuant software (v3.0.3) based on linear calibration curves. Fecal bile acid profiling was performed by MetWare (http://www.metware.cn/) based on the AB Sciex QTRAP 6500 LC-MS/MS platform. A detailed list of MRM transitions, collision energies, retention times, and mass spectra for all targeted bile acids is provided in Supplementary Data 4.

For targeted fecal bile acid metabolomics, orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) was performed using the R (v4.4.1) package ropls (v1.36.0) for pairwise comparisons between the indicated groups (n = 6 per group). Differential metabolites were defined as those with a variable importance in projection (VIP) > 1 and |log₂ fold change| > 1 between the indicated groups. Score plots and heatmaps were generated with ggplot2 (v3.5.2) and pheatmap (v1.0.12), respectively (Fig. 6d–g). Intersection analysis of differential metabolites was conducted with the Evenn online tool (https://www.bic.ac.cn/test/venn/#/) and visualized as a Venn diagram (Fig. 6h). KEGG pathway enrichment results were displayed as bubble plots using ggplot2 (v3.5.2) (Fig. 6i), and quantitative data for key differential metabolites were plotted as bar graphs in GraphPad Prism v10 (Fig. 6k).

Statistics and reproducibility
Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism v10 and R software (v4.4.1). Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM), as indicated in the figure legends. Data distribution was assessed for normality. Comparisons between two groups were conducted using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests or Mann–Whitney U-tests. For comparisons among more than two groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test or Kruskal–Wallis tests followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test were applied. To correct for multiple testing in large-scale datasets (e.g., metabolomics and transcriptomics), the False Discovery Rate (FDR) was controlled using the Benjamini–Krieger–Yekutieli two-stage step-up method (or the Benjamini–Hochberg method for RNA-seq).

Specific R packages were employed for data visualization and analysis, including ggplot2 (v3.5.2) for general plotting, ggradar (v0.2) for radar plots, pheatmap (v1.0.12) for heatmaps, ggsignif (v0.6.4) for significance annotation, and vegan (v2.6-10) for diversity analysis. All schematic diagrams were created using BioRender (Zhang, J. (2026) https://BioRender.com/3qyx3m3). All experiments were performed with at least three independent biological replicates to ensure reproducibility.

### Reviewer 2

Recommendation: Major Revision
This manuscript presents a novel and compelling approach to probiotic optimization through host-mediated directed evolution. The concept of using the gut as a living bioreactor to select for functionally enhanced probiotics is innovative and holds significant translational potential, particularly in the context of NAFLD. The multi-omics integration and functional validation of key mutations are strengths. However, several major concerns must be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication.
Major Concerns:
1.Lack of mechanistic causality between mutations and phenotype. While the two SNVs (rs1846941 and rs402499) are associated with enhanced bile acid metabolism, direct evidence of causality is limited. Perform complementation or knockout experiments in the parental strain to confirm that these mutations alone are sufficient to confer the enhanced phenotype.
2.Insufficient characterization of the adapted strain’s ecological impact. The metagenomic data show no major shifts in community structure between HFAD-H22B656 and HFAD-WSS9 groups, but functional changes in the microbiome (e.g., BSH activity of other taxa) are not assessed. Include functional metagenomics or metatranscriptomics to evaluate whether WSS9 influences the bile acid metabolism of other gut microbes.
3.Limited assessment of long-term stability and safety. The adapted strain was evaluated in an 8-week intervention, but the genetic stability of the mutations under prolonged colonization or in complex microbiota is not tested. Include a stability assay (e.g., serial passaging in vitro or in vivo without selection pressure) to assess whether the mutations revert or confer unintended traits.
4.Incomplete translation to human relevance. The study relies solely on a mouse model. The applicability of this approach to human microbiomes remains speculative. Discuss limitations and propose future steps, such as using humanized gnotobiotic models or organoids, to enhance translational relevance.
5.Statistical and methodological clarifications needed. Some figure captions and methods lack detail (e.g., n-values, statistical tests used in metabolomics, multiple testing correction in RNA-seq). Provide full statistical details in figure legends and methods. Ensure that all comparisons are appropriately corrected for multiple testing.
Minor Concerns:
1.Figure 3e: The schematic of bile acid metabolism is helpful but could be better annotated with gene names and pathways.
2.The discussion section could be more concise and focused on the broader implications of the work beyond NAFLD.
3.Please clarify whether the adapted strain was tested for any off-target effects (e.g., growth kinetics, biofilm production, antibiotic resistance, virulence factors, or other traits).

### Reviewer 3

This is a very interesting topic with the potential for application to address issues in human health and disease. The main premise of the study is to determine whether the “host gut … could serve as a bioreactor for the directed evolution of probiotic strains”. The authors utilize a probiotic strain of Bifidobacterium animalis with intrinsic bile acid-metabolizing capacity. When an in vivo approach was taken in germ-free mice under bile-acid stress, the probiotic strain exhibited an increase in bile acid metabolism whereas in vitro evolution methods failed to produce any functional gains. The authors identified 2 single nucleotide variants that could explain the enhanced bile acid metabolism in the adapted strain. They go on to show the functional relevance of the adapted strains in a diet-induced mouse model of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).
The noteworthy results include the efficacy of the in vivo induction strategy for enhancing bile acid-metabolism, the identification and functional validation of two SNVs that potentially confer the enhanced bile acid metabolism. The data presented with respect to the two SNVs is for the most part convincing. However, effects of the two SNVs on enhanced bile acid metabolism seems over-interpreted in some sections and needs clarification in other areas. I think where the findings could also be strengthened is in the studies focusing on the translational potential in the NAFLD model.
Main comments:
Figure 4d: The authors state that “mdr expression was significantly higher in the mdr-N192D under all bile acid conditions”. While that might be accurate at the 3h time point, it does not fully describe the data shown about mdr expression going down from baseline for both WT and N192D variant following induction with cholic acid CA and chenodeoxycholic acid CDCA. In addition, the followup sentence “Together, these results demonstrate that the N192D substitution upregulates mdr expression” isn’t entirely accurate…could this statement be revised given that the variant upregulates mdr expression to a greater degree after induction specifically with deoxycholic acid induction and not with CA or CDCA? The second half of the statement “potentially by altering local mRNA secondary structure (thus enhancing ribosome binding or translation initiation), optimizing codon usage bias, modulating mRNA folding dynamics or modifying regulatory elements affecting splicing translation” seems overly speculative.
Line items 272-273: in the results section, it states “N192D mutation stabilizes the protein-substrate complex, thereby facilitating more efficient substrate recognition and transmembrane transport” is declarative without evidence…would it be more accurate to state “…complex, potentially facilitating more efficient substrate recognition…”?
Adapted strain on weight gain: The three parameters chosen are useful outcome measurements to gauge the effect of the adapted strains. However, what could be clarified is the main comparison of interest. In the weight gain figure (Figure 5c), the authors state the HFAD-W5S9 treated mice showed the smallest weight gain from control, followed by the parental strain treated mice. The effect size of the adapted strain is not immediately accessible to the reader. What is the absolute difference in effect?…did it prevent weight gain imposed by a HFD by 30%, 50%, etc. and how does that compare to the parental strain? The results section could be rewritten to clarify this point.
Adapted strain on liver histology: It would be helpful to perform semi-quantitative scoring for histology and oil red O staining across samples within each group to get a more accurate assessment of the adapted strain’s impact, if any, on the liver. This is critical as non-alcoholic steatohepatitis rests ultimately on histologic diagnosis. Response to 1.2: Thank you for your valuable suggestion. In accordance with this recommendation, we have now incorporated quantitative measurements of Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 and its adapted derivative W5S9 in fecal samples. In this study, two experimental components are directly related to bacterial colonization. Below, we describe how colonization was established and quantitatively assessed in each component:
First, in the strain adaptation experiment, to exclude the interference of endogenous microbiota, we used germ-free mice as evolutionary biological reactors to establish a colonization model of Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis H22B656. Each mouse was gavaged with 200 μL of bacterial suspension containing 10⁹ CFU daily for 3 consecutive days, thereby establishing a single-strain colonization model in the germ-free mice.
Second, to evaluate the beneficial potential of the adaptive strain Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis W5S9 in modulating host metabolism, we established a diet-induced non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) model in SPF mice. The animals were randomly assigned to four groups (n = 6 per group): control, HFAD, HFAD-H22B656, and HFAD-W5S9. 1.4 Is there any data supporting the impact of H22B656 on the intestinal wall of animals (The level of IL-6? 10? TNF-a?)?
Response to 1.4: Thank you for your insightful comment regarding the impact of Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 on intestinal barrier integrity and local immune status. In this study, we evaluated the anti-inflammatory efficacy of the original strain H22B656 and the adapted strain W5S9 by quantifying serum levels of key pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6 and TNF-α).
It is well established that in high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity models, systemic inflammation is primarily driven by impaired intestinal barrier function and the subsequent translocation of endotoxins (e.g., lipopolysaccharide, LPS) into the circulation 1. This establishes a direct correlation between elevated serum inflammatory markers and intestinal barrier dysfunction 2, 3. Therefore, although intestinal tissue was not directly sampled in our experiment, the aforementioned pathophysiology supports the use of the serum cytokine profile as a robust proxy for both intestinal barrier integrity and local inflammatory status. Furthermore, elevated levels of IL-6 and TNF-α are well documented to play a pivotal role in disrupting the intestinal mucosal barrier and increasing intestinal permeability 4. Specifically, TNF-α has been shown to promote the degradation of tight junction proteins, such as occludin and members of the claudin family, thereby compromising barrier integrity 2, 3. Concurrently, IL-6 increases epithelial permeability by upregulating the pore-forming protein claudin-2, further impairing the intestinal barrier 4. Therefore, reducing the levels or activity of these pro-inflammatory cytokines is critical for preserving intestinal structural integrity.
In our study, supplementation with both the original strain H22B656 and the adapted strain W5S9 significantly reduced serum IL-6 and TNF-α levels compared with the HFAD group (p < 0.05), restoring cytokine levels to those observed in the control group (Fig. 5f). Based on the aforementioned mechanisms, this marked decrease in systemic inflammatory markers strongly suggests that H22B656 mitigates inflammatory stress and thereby preserves intestinal barrier integrity. Although no significant difference was detected between W5S9 and H22B656 in terms of cytokine regulation, both strains exerted significantly stronger anti-inflammatory effects than the HFAD group. The comparable efficacy of W5S9 and H22B656 indicates that the domestication process did not compromise the strain’s functional activity. Collectively, these findings underscore the therapeutic potential of H22B656 in modulating gut-associated immune responses and promoting intestinal health.

1.5 At the final time point, were intestinal segments tissue responsible for metabolizing secondary bile acids collected? And to assess the activation status of relevant targets and the network between bacteria, fermented substances, and the host?
Response to 1.5: Thank you for your valuable comments. We would like to begin by clarifying a key concept regarding secondary bile acid metabolism. The biotransformation of primary into secondary bile acids (e.g., deconjugation and 7α-dehydroxylation) is predominantly driven by enzymes secreted by gut microorganisms (such as bile salt hydrolase) within the intestinal lumen, rather than by intestinal epithelial tissues themselves 5, 6. Therefore, to accurately investigate this critical metabolic process, we focused our analyses on colonic contents (fecal samples), which constitute the actual microenvironment where microbial fermentation and secondary bile acid production occur.
Unfortunately, intestinal tissues were not collected at the final time point of this study for the assessment of local bile acid metabolism or the activation of receptors such as FXR and TGR5. To systematically evaluate the “bacteria–metabolites–host” network, we employed a multi-omics strategy. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was used to characterize the microbial taxa involved in bile acid metabolism and to annotate key functional genes (e.g., BSH), thereby elucidating the potential mechanisms of bile acid transformation at both the taxonomic and functional levels. Targeted bile acid metabolomics was applied to accurately quantify primary and secondary bile acids. Given that secondary bile acids can influence whole-body metabolic status through the gut–liver axis, we operationally defined “host target activation” as alterations in systemic physiological and biochemical parameters, as well as hepatic histopathology, to reflect the distal regulatory effects mediated via the gut–liver axis.
In response, we expanded and refined the correlation analysis and constructed multi-omics association networks integrating microbial taxa, functional genes, bile acid metabolites, and host metabolic indicators in both the original and adapted strain groups (Spearman rank correlation, r > 0.6, p < 0.05). These results are summarized in a new supplementary figure (Fig. S8), which illustrates the expanded multi-omics correlation patterns and provides a more systematic view of their interrelationships. In the HFAD-H22B656 group, Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 showed significant correlations with 59 intestinal microbial taxa, indicating robust colonization capacity. However, its regulatory network along the “microbe–metabolite–host” functional axis appeared relatively limited. It was primarily associated with secondary bile acids such as TDCA (taurodeoxycholic acid ， r=-0.6989,p=0.0167) and 7-KLCA (7-ketolithocholic acid, r=-0.6097, p=0.0464), and exhibited significant negative correlations with pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, r=-0.7485, p=0.0081 and IL-6 r=-0.8080, p=0.0026), suggesting a degree of anti-inflammatory potential. Nonetheless, its correlations with key indicators of hepatic injury (such as AST) were relatively weak, indicating that the original strain had limited capacity to reshape the bile acid profile or ameliorate NAFLD-related metabolic damage. In contrast, the domesticated strain W5S9 exhibited pronounced functional rewiring within its network structure. Most notably, W5S9 showed a strong positive correlation with the BSH functional gene, indicating enhanced bile salt-hydrolyzing potential (BSH, r=0.6681, p=0.0176). Moreover, the bile acid profile of the domesticated-strain group underwent qualitative shifts, with W5S9 exhibiting significant negative correlations with key bile acids such as TCDCA (Taurochenodeoxycholic acid, r=-0.6905, p=0.0129) and TCA (Taurocholic acid, r=-0.6569, p=0.0203), suggesting a stronger modulatory influence on bile acid transformation pathways. At the host level, W5S9 not only retained its inhibitory correlations with inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α , r=-0.6532, p=0.0213 and IL-6, r=-0.7241, p=0.0078), but also showed significant negative correlations with key NAFLD-related pathological indicators (AST, r=-0.6799, p=0.01519 and LDL-C, r=-0.69429, p=0.0123), indicating a markedly enhanced capacity to modulate the bile acid profile and improve host metabolic outcomes.
In summary, by performing a systematic correlation analysis that integrates metagenomics, targeted bile acid metabolomics, and systemic host indices, we have constructed a comprehensive multi-omics network. This network holistically elucidates the interaction patterns among the gut microbiota, bile acid metabolism, and host metabolic responses. While we acknowledge the absence of data regarding local receptor activation in intestinal tissues, the current multi-dimensional dataset provides robust evidence to support our key inferences regarding the “Bacteria-Substance-Host” axis. We have explicitly addressed this limitation in the Discussion section and plan to further validate local signaling pathways via transcriptomics and proteomics in future studies.

Response to 1.7: Thank you for this important question. We fully understand the reviewer’s concern regarding the unexpectedly high Shannon diversity index shown in Figure 6. We would like to clarify that the data presented in Figure 6 were derived from the efficacy-validation experiment conducted in SPF (specific pathogen-free) mice, rather than from the germ-free (GF) mice used for in vivo strain adaptation. To avoid confusion, we hereby clarify that the current study design comprises two independent animal experiments:
1. Host-mediated adaptive induction strategy for probiotic strains (using Germ-Free mice)
Germ-free (GF) mice were employed to establish an “in vivo evolutionary bioreactor” to eliminate interference from any endogenous microbiota. Monocolonization was established via oral gavage of 10⁹ CFU of B. animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 daily for three consecutive days, followed by a 7-week in vivo adaptation process under a stepwise high-fat, high-cholesterol diet. As the mice remained monocolonized throughout this experiment, this phase naturally did not yield data showing elevated Shannon diversity.
2. Efficacy Evaluation of the Adapted Strain (Using SPF Mice; Source of Data for Figure 6)
To evaluate the preventive effect of the adapted probiotic B. animalis subsp. lactis W5S9 on non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), we conducted an experiment using specific pathogen-free (SPF) mice. In this experiment, mice were randomly assigned to four groups (n=6 per group): Control Group: Fed a normal diet and administered 200 μL of sterile saline via oral gavage; HFAD Group: Fed a high-fat diet (HFAD) and administered 200 μL of sterile saline via oral gavage; HFAD-H22B656 Group: Fed a high-fat diet and administered 200 μL of sterile saline containing 109CFU of the original strain B. animalis subsp. lactis H22B656; HFAD-W5S9 Group: Fed a high-fat diet and administered 200 μL of sterile saline containing 109 CFU of the adapted strain B. animalis subsp. lactis W5S9. Following an 8-week intervention, fecal samples were collected for metagenomic sequencing, while serum biochemical indices and liver pathological changes were assessed. Notably, a significant increase in the Shannon diversity index was primarily observed in the HFAD-H22B656 and HFAD-W5S9 groups, indicating that probiotic colonization significantly improved gut microbiota diversity against the background of a high-fat diet (Figure 6a in the manuscript).
To further elucidate specific alterations in the bacterial communities, we conducted a detailed taxonomic analysis of the gut microbiota at both the genus and species levels. These results are presented in the newly added Supplementary Figure S3 In terms of overall composition (Fig. S3b), the HFAD group exhibited a distinct shift in microbial structure compared to the Control group. However, intervention with strains H22B656 and W5S9 effectively remodeled the gut microbiota, restoring the compositional profile to a state resembling that of the Control group, particularly regarding the relative abundances of Lachnospiraceae and Muribaculaceae. Further analysis at the species level revealed that the HFAD phenotype was characterized by a depletion of potentially beneficial taxa, such as members of Muribaculaceae (e.g., Muribaculaceae bacterium Isolate 104, Muribaculaceae intestinale) and Paramuribaculum intestinale, concomitant with an enrichment of certain unclassified taxa (e.g., GGB28695, GGB27768). Notably, treatment with both H22B656 and W5S9 successfully reversed these dysbiotic patterns, restoring the abundance of species associated with Muribaculaceae and Bacteroidaceae to levels comparable to the Control group (Fig. S3c, d). We subsequently compared the differential taxa between the two probiotic intervention groups, and differential abundance analysis revealed no significant differences in the abundance of key species, including Bifidobacterium animalis (q-value > 0.05; Fig. S3e). This suggests that both strains exert similar beneficial regulatory effects on gut microbiota composition. Finally, to prevent potential misinterpretation and enhance clarity, we have included a comprehensive experimental schematic in Figure 1, which details the workflow of the study design.

Response: We sincerely thank Reviewer #1 for reviewing our manuscript and for their positive feedback on our work. In the following sections, we will address each comment and suggestion made by the reviewer, and the changes in the manuscript are highlighted in green.
Major Concerns:
2.1 Lack of mechanistic causality between mutations and phenotype. While the two SNVs (rs1846941 and rs402499) are associated with enhanced bile acid metabolism, direct evidence of causality is limited. Perform complementation or knockout experiments in the parental strain to confirm that these mutations alone are sufficient to confer the enhanced phenotype.
Response to 2.1: Thank you for your thorough review and valuable feedback on our study. Regarding your concern about the “lack of mechanistic causality between the mutations and phenotype,” we understand your concern and have taken additional experimental steps to validate the mechanism of the mutations. To investigate the causal impact of these mutations on the phenotype, we performed gene knockout and complementation experiments in both the parental strain Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 and the adapted strain Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis W5S9. These experiments were designed to directly verify whether these two mutations are sufficient to confer the enhanced bile acid metabolism phenotype independently.
For rs1846941, we knocked out the cbh promoter region where the mutation is located and then assessed the expression of cbh under three different bile salt conditions (0.3% deoxycholic acid (DCA), cholic acid (CA) and chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) to explore whether this promoter region regulates gene expression. The results showed that under all three bile salt conditions (DCA, CA, and CDCA), the expression of cbh in the wild-type adapted strain was significantly higher than in the original wild-type strain, suggesting that this non-coding mutation enhances cbh transcription under bile acid stress (fold changes of 1.65, 1.51, and 1.49 for DCA, CA, and CDCA, respectively; One-way ANOVA with Tukey’s HSD test, p < 0.01; Fig. 4d). More importantly, after knocking out the promoter sequence, cbh expression was abolished, further confirming that the upregulation of cbh in the adapted strain is indeed attributed to this non-coding mutation.
Additionally, we performed a resazurin assay to evaluate the hydrolytic activity of bile salts in different strains to assess the impact of the promoter sequence on bile salt hydrolysis (Fig. 4e). The results showed that for glycine-conjugated bile salts, the wild-type adapted strain exhibited significantly higher hydrolytic activity than the wild-type original strain. After knocking out the mutation site, both strains lost the ability to hydrolyze glycine-conjugated bile salts. For taurine-conjugated bile salts, the hydrolytic activity of the adapted strain remained higher than that of the original strain, regardless of whether the strain was wild-type or knockout. These findings demonstrate that the non-coding mutation in the cbh promoter region enhances bile salt hydrolysis, particularly in the hydrolysis of glycine- and taurine-conjugated bile salts, by regulating the expression of the cbh gene.
For rs402499, we similarly performed a knockout of the mdr gene at the mutation site and examined mdr expression under three different bile salt conditions (0.3% deoxycholic acid (DCA), cholic acid (CA) and chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA)) to verify whether this mutation directly affects gene expression levels. Under DCA, CA, and CDCA treatment conditions, the mdr expression in the wild-type adapted strain was significantly higher than in the parental wild-type strain, suggesting that this locus significantly enhances mdr transcription in response to bile salt stress (fold changes of 1.74, 2.13, and 1.62 for DCA, CA, and CDCA, respectively; One-way ANOVA with Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test, p < 0.01; Fig. 4f). Further analysis showed that knockout of the mdr gene led to a marked reduction in its expression, indicating that rs402499 directly contributes to the phenotype by regulating mdr transcription. Additionally, we performed complementation experiments to verify whether the restoration of the mdr gene could recover the phenotype. Under CA, DCA and CDCA treatment conditions, the mdr expression in the complemented adapted strain was significantly higher than that in the wild-type complemented strain (p < 0.01; Fig. 4f). These findings suggest that the rs402499 (N192D) mutation drives adaptive phenotypes by increasing mdr expression under bile acid stress.
Mdr, as a transporter protein, can efflux free bile acids, thereby alleviating the toxicity of bile salt molecules to the strain and improving survival 8. To further validate the causal relationship between mdr gene expression and phenotype, we measured the viable bacterial counts of different strains under bile salt stress (p < 0.01; Fig. 4g). The experimental results showed that, under all three bile salt conditions, the colony counts of the wild-type adapted strain were significantly higher than those of the parental wild-type strain. Notably, under CA and CDCA treatment, the mdr knockout strains exhibited a marked growth disadvantage, whereas the differences between knockout strains were less pronounced under DCA conditions (ns). In the complementation experiment, the complemented adapted strain showed significantly higher colony counts than the wild-type parental strain, further supporting the functional role of the mdr gene under bile salt stress. Overall, the mutation in the mdr gene (rs402499) significantly impacted bile acid metabolism and the growth ability of the strain, further confirming the causal relationship between the mutation and the phenotype.
In conclusion, gene knockout and complementation experiments provided functional validation of the causal relationship between the non-coding mutations rs1846941 and rs402499 and the associated phenotypic changes. We found that these mutations not only caused significant changes in gene expression but also directly influenced bile salt metabolism and the survival ability of the strains under bile salt stress. Specifically, the non-coding mutation in the cbh promoter region enhanced bile salt hydrolysis activity, while the mutation in the mdr gene improved bile salt transport and strain tolerance. 2) Revised Materials and Methods Section:
Line 763-791:
Construction of gene knockout and complemented strains
To establish a causal relationship between the rs1846941 and rs402499 mutations and the phenotype of interest, we employed a homologous recombination strategy using the temperature-sensitive suicide plasmid pKO403 to generate deletion mutants targeting the mdr and cbh promoter regions in both the parental strain Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis H22B656 and the adapted strain B. animalis subsp. lactis W5S9.Genomic DNA from the respective strains was used as the template to amplify the upstream and downstream homologous arms flanking the mdr and cbh promoter regions by PCR using primers listed in Supplementary Table 2. Amplicons were resolved by agarose gel electrophoresis and purified. The pKO403 plasmid was linearized by double digestion with SalI and BamHI and seamlessly assembled with the purified homologous arms using 2×Ezmax® Universal CloneMix (37 °C, 30 min). Assembly products were transformed into E. coli DH5α competent cells, and recombinant plasmids were identified by colony PCR. Plasmids confirmed by PCR were isolated and electroporated into electrocompetent H22B656 and W5S9 cells (2.1 kV, 200 Ω, 25 μF). Following electroporation, cells were recovered in 1 mL MRS-cys medium under anaerobic conditions at 37 °C for 4 h and plated on MRS-cys agar containing chloramphenicol (10 μg/mL) to select for single-crossover integrants. Chloramphenicol-resistant colonies were cultured in MRS-cys broth supplemented with chloramphenicol (10 μg/mL) at 37 °C for 48 h and subsequently plated on MRS-cys agar with chloramphenicol for anaerobic incubation at 42 °C for 48 h to promote double-crossover recombination. Successful deletion of the target region was confirmed by PCR, and double-crossover deletion mutants were obtained. To eliminate the pKO403 plasmid, verified mutants were passaged for three consecutive generations in antibiotic-free MRS-cys medium.
For complementation of the Δmdr mutant, a 1,648-bp fragment containing the full-length mdr gene and its native promoter was PCR-amplified from the genomic DNA of H22B656 or W5S9 using primers listed in Supplementary Table 2 and cloned into SalI/BamHI-digested pKO403. The resulting plasmid was introduced into the Δmdr strain by electroporation, and transformants were selected on MRS-cys agar containing chloramphenicol (10 μg/mL). Successful construction of complemented strains was confirmed by PCR.

Response to 2.2: We appreciate your insightful comments regarding functional ecological impact. To specifically distinguish the direct enzymatic contribution of the supplemented strains from potential regulatory effects on the resident microbiota, we performed functional profiling of the metagenomic data using HUMAnN v3.9 to quantify the abundance of bile salt hydrolase (EC 3.5.1.24) encoding genes, and incorporated these new results into Supplementary Figure S6. Our analysis revealed that the total abundance of BSH-encoding genes was markedly higher in the HFAD-W5S9 group compared with the HFAD-H22B656 group, which is consistent with the improved bile acid metabolic phenotype observed in the host fecal targeted bile acid metabolomics (Fig. S6a).
To further evaluate whether W5S9 induces functional remodeling among background taxa, we additionally performed a stratified contribution analysis, which partitions BSH activity by microbial origin. Notably, the BSH contribution from the endogenous gut microbiota remained largely unchanged between the two groups (Fig. S6b, c), indicating that the elevated BSH capacity is predominantly driven by the colonization and enzymatic expression of W5S9, rather than by extensive functional rewiring of the resident community. These findings indicate that the marked enhancement of total BSH capacity is predominantly attributable to the direct colonization and enzymatic activity of the adapted W5S9 strain itself, thereby conferring a more efficient bile acid transformation phenotype to the gut ecosystem without inducing substantial dysbiosis or functional disturbance within the endogenous microbial community.

2.3 Limited assessment of long-term stability and safety. The adapted strain was evaluated in an 8-week intervention, but the genetic stability of the mutations under prolonged colonization or in complex microbiota is not tested. Include a stability assay (e.g., serial passaging in vitro or in vivo without selection pressure) to assess whether the mutations revert or confer unintended traits.
Response to 2.3：Thank you for your valuable comments regarding the long-term stability and safety of the strain. To address these concerns, we performed a rigorous long-term serial passage assay followed by whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Specifically, the adapted strain W5S9 were subjected to daily serial passaging for 4 weeks under two conditions: (i) a non-selective medium (MRS broth supplemented with L-cysteine hydrochloride), used to assess stability in the absence of selection pressure; and (ii) a selective medium (MRS broth supplemented with bile salts and L-cysteine hydrochloride), used to mimic gut environmental pressure. Target strains were re-isolated weekly, genomic DNA was extracted, and WGS was performed to monitor potential genetic changes. The whole-genome sequencing data of the isolates have been deposited in the NCBI database under BioProject accession number PRJNA1380636.
Throughout the 4-week passaging period, the identified key SNVs (rs1846941 and rs402499) in the W5S9 strain were maintained at 100% frequency, regardless of whether the medium was selective or non-selective. No reversion to the wild-type genotype was observed, demonstrating that these mutations possess high genetic stability even in the absence of ecological selection pressure (Figure S4a, b).
We also wish to clarify that in therapeutic applications, probiotics are typically administered via continuous or semi-continuous dosing, ensuring that the strain ingested daily remains consistent and stable. We have successfully demonstrated phenotypic persistence in our 8-week in vivo study involving continuous administration (The HFAD-W5S9 group received 200 μL of sterile saline containing 10⁹ CFU of the adapted strain W5S9 daily for eight weeks.). Taken together with the new in vitro stability data, we provide robust evidence that W5S9 retains its beneficial properties without undergoing genetic drift within the relevant intervention timeframe.

2.4 Incomplete translation to human relevance. The study relies solely on a mouse model. The applicability of this approach to human microbiomes remains speculative. Discuss limitations and propose future steps, such as using humanized gnotobiotic models or organoids, to enhance translational relevance.
Response to 2.4: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding translational relevance. While the murine model used here enables controlled mechanistic evaluation of bile acid metabolism and host signaling, we recognize that differences in gut ecology and physiology limit direct extrapolation to humans. We have now expanded the Discussion to clearly acknowledge this limitation and to highlight strategies that enhance the translational bridge to human application.
Specifically, although the overall microbiome composition differs between mice and humans, the core molecular pathways involved in bile acid metabolism (e.g., BSH-mediated deconjugation) and host signaling (FXR/TGR5) are evolutionarily conserved across both species 9, 10. This conservation suggests that the principal mechanisms underlying the effects of the adapted strain are likely to be cross-species applicable, thereby providing a biological rationale for its future clinical translation.
To strengthen translational relevance, we now provide a concrete future research roadmap involving two complementary human-relevant systems:1. Humanized Gnotobiotic Murine Models: By transplanting fecal microbiota from specific cohorts (e.g., patients with hyperlipidemia) into germ-free mice, we aim to evaluate the colonization dynamics and metabolic regulatory capacity of the adapted strain within a human-derived microbial ecology, thereby more accurately recapitulating the human physiological environment.2. Human Intestinal Organoid Systems: We plan to utilize ex vivo human intestinal organoids to directly assess the strain's impact on epithelial barrier function and relevant signaling pathways. This approach will allow us to circumvent limitations imposed by species-specific differences and enhance the physiological relevance of our translational assessment. Together, these future studies will substantially enhance the human translational foundation of our adapted-strain strategy while preserving the mechanistic strengths of the current work. We believe that the present findings provide an essential proof-of-concept for host-guided probiotic optimization and justify continued clinical-oriented development.

(e) Conjugated primary bile acids are taken up by bacteria and undergo deconjugation by bile salt hydrolase (cbh), releasing taurine or glycine and generating free cholic acid (CA) and chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA). Free primary bile acids may passively diffuse across the cell membrane or be extruded by efflux transporters (e.g., Mdr, LmrA). Within bacterial cells, oxidoreductive reactions mediated by 7β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (7β-HSDH/hdhA) convert CA and CDCA into intermediates such as UCA and UDCA. Subsequently, multi-step 7α-dehydroxylation catalyzed by the bai gene cluster (baiA/baiB/baiCD/baiE) transforms these intermediates into the secondary bile acids deoxycholic acid (DCA) and lithocholic acid (LCA). Transporters such as BaiG and BaiF mediate the export of secondary bile acids into the extracellular space. Red arrows denote steps involved in primary bile acid processing, whereas blue arrows highlight secondary bile acid biosynthesis.

Response to 2.7: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestion. In response, we have streamlined the Discussion by reducing repetitive NAFLD-specific descriptions and have revised the concluding paragraph to more clearly emphasize the broader implications of our host-mediated in vivo induction strategy beyond NAFLD. 1) Revised Discussion section (line 487-505):
Importantly, this host-mediated in vivo induction strategy is not restricted to NAFLD but can be broadly generalized to other probiotic functions and disease indications. By rationally tuning host background, diet, and environmental stressors, the gut can be used as a programmable evolutionary bioreactor to enrich for strains that are optimized for distinct therapeutic tasks. For instance, strains could be adapted in inflammatory or epithelial-injury models to bolster gut barrier restoration and mucosal immune regulation, thereby potentially benefiting inflammatory bowel disease, post-antibiotic gut dysfunction, or complications following chemotherapy and radiotherapy11. Likewise, when evolved under dietary fiber-enriched or prebiotic-supplemented conditions, probiotics might acquire high short-chain fatty acid–producing capacity and refined signaling properties, making them attractive adjuncts for metabolic, cardiovascular, or neuropsychiatric disorders in which gut–brain and gut–liver axes are involved12, 13. Furthermore, applying selective pressures linked to xenobiotic degradation or drug metabolism could yield strains with enhanced capabilities for therapeutic compound modulation or detoxification, broadening their utility in pharmaco-microbiomics and microbiome-based drug-response optimization14. Beyond single-trait enhancement, combining this platform with multi-strain consortia or personalized dietary regimens may ultimately enable patient-specific, functionally tailored live biotherapeutic products that extend well beyond liver disease and provide a generalizable route to next-generation microbiome therapeutics.

Response: We fully appreciate your concerns regarding the safety and stability of the adapted strain. First, it is important to highlight that the parental strain, Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis, is formally listed in the “List of Microorganisms Allowed for Use in Food” in China and has been granted Qualified Presumption of Safety (QPS) status by the European Union. Consequently, it possesses a well-established history of safe use in food products and dietary supplements. Secondly, to directly determine whether the adaptation process introduced any off-target effects, we performed a comprehensive evaluation of the adapted strain across four key dimensions: growth performance (growth kinetics), colonization potential (biofilm formation), antibiotic susceptibility (minimum inhibitory concentrations, MICs), and virulence-associated safety.
With respect to growth performance, we carried out a 48-h in vitro growth-curve assay. The adapted strain W5S9 exhibited growth kinetics (lag phase, exponential phase, and stationary-phase biomass) that were indistinguishable from those of the parental strain, indicating that metabolic adaptation did not impose a detectable fitness cost on bacterial growth (Fig. S5a). With regard to colonization potential, biofilm formation was quantified after 12 h of incubation using a crystal-violet assay. No significant difference in biofilm biomass was observed between W5S9 and the parental strain H22B656, suggesting that the adaptive evolution process did not compromise the strain’s intrinsic adhesion or colonization properties (Fig. S5b).
To assess antibiotic resistance, we first performed genomic annotation of the parental strain using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD)15. This analysis identified two well-characterized tetracycline resistance genes, tet(W) and tet(M), both encoding ribosomal protection proteins that confer resistance to tetracycline-class antibiotics such as tetracycline and doxycycline16 (Fig. S5c). We then determined the minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of tetracycline and doxycycline for both the parental and adapted strains, and observed identical susceptibility profiles (Fig. S5d). These results confirm that the in vivo adaptation process did not alter the antibiotic susceptibility of the adapted strain W5S9. In parallel, we evaluated virulence-associated safety. Whole-genome annotation using the Virulence Factor Database (VFDB) confirmed the absence of functional toxin-encoding genes, including hemolysins and cytolysins, in the genome of the parental strain H22B65617.
Taken together, our systematic evaluation (encompassing physiology, colonization, antibiotic susceptibility, and genomic safety) confirms that the adaptation process enhanced metabolic function without inducing off-target effects or compromising safety. Here, we would like to further elaborate on the differential efficacy between the parental and adapted strains. While the parental strain H22B656 exerts beneficial effects on bile acid metabolism, the adapted strain W5S9 demonstrates a substantially stronger capacity to restore bile acid homeostasis. In particular, W5S9 more effectively reduces the HFAD-induced elevations of conjugated bile acids such as TCDCA and TCA, bringing their levels closer to those of the healthy control group (Fig. 6k; Fig. S7). These findings highlight the functional enhancement conferred by host-mediated adaptation and underscore the superior robustness of W5S9 in correcting HFAD-associated metabolic disturbances.
